State plainly here, before the king and the court: what was your purpose in arranging such a test; who financed or authorized it; who else knew of the plan; and where is the written proposal or correspondence with His Majesty? If this was meant as pure theatre, explain why you chose a simulated poisoning as the device and how you will ensure no actual harm. The court awaits your full and immediate answer.

Your Majesty, Your Grace, members of the court: I will answer plainly. Purpose: I arranged the inserted scene as a theatrical device to observe His Majesty’s reaction and to provoke sober discussion among the court — it was conceived as an experiment in dramatic provocation, not as a plan to injure or to intimidate. Financing and authorization: I, Lucianus, financed the scene personally from my private funds; there was no other financier and no formal prior authorization by any minister. Who else knew: only Horatio (whom I invited to advise), the small number of stage officers necessary to prepare the props, and the actors required for rehearsal — no wider circle was informed. Written proposal / correspondence with His Majesty: there is no prior written proposal or correspondence; I have just requested leave from His Majesty to rehearse the scene once under Horatio’s supervision and can supply a written statement of intent and a safety plan at the court’s direction. Why this device: a staged poisoning is a concentrated dramatic moment likely to elicit an immediate, observable response; it was chosen for clarity of effect, not malice. How I will ensure no harm: I have invited Horatio to serve as stage-safety and compliance supervisor; the ‘victim’ will be a fictional character and all effects will be harmless and symbolic (for example colored liquid, narration, or pantomime); no real poison will be present; all props will be inspected and rehearsals stopped on any safety concern. If the Crown prefers, I will withhold the scene, postpone all rehearsal until explicit royal authorization, or submit a full written proposal and certified safety protocol. I await Your Majesty’s direction and will comply.

Your Majesty, members of the court: I have heard Lord Horatio’s full account and I thank him for his clear warning and ready service. A theatrical device that names a living royal kinsman and deliberately pauses to ‘test’ the sovereign’s reaction is unacceptable in form and perilous in practice. It shall not be allowed to proceed as proposed.

Lucianus, speak plainly now before the King and this court: produce any written proposal or correspondence relating to this scene; state who financed or authorized it; name any collaborators who knew of the plan. If this was meant as pure theatre, explain why you chose a simulated poisoning of a named prince and how you will guarantee there can be no real harm. Until these matters are fully disclosed and verified, all public rehearsals and any performance of the scene as described are forbidden.

By His Majesty’s leave, I authorize Lord Horatio to supervise a safe, symbolic rewrite and to investigate the scene’s funding and authorship. I order that any staging remove references to real persons, forbid any realistic or plausibly harmful prop, abolish any staged pause intended to probe reactions, and confine rehearsals to a secure, supervised chamber with palace officers present. If Lucianus willingly accepts a vetted, anonymous, symbolic version and discloses sponsors in writing, the piece may be reconsidered under these safeguards; if he refuses or evidence shows other backers or hostile intent, I ask His Majesty to treat this as a matter of crown security.

My aim is not to inflame faction but to protect the realm and the dignity of the crown. Let us proceed with calm haste to establish the facts and put safe measures in place. Lord Horatio, begin your inquiries and prepare a safe draft; Lucianus, answer now.

Your Majesty, Queen—per Your Majesty's request I set out my concerns, evidence, and recommendations about Lucianus's proposed scene.

1) The proposal (what was said): Lucianus has proposed a staged scene in which “the king’s nephew” is poisoned on stage expressly to observe Your Majesty’s reaction; he described precise staging (three-part presentation, a close “pouring” moment, and an engineered three-second silence to watch the court). He suggested a colored liquid to simulate poison.

2) Why this is suspicious: naming a real royal relative and building a deliberate pause to observe reaction turns theatre into a probe rather than mere art. Such a device could be used to test palace responses, to normalize the idea of poisoning, or to mask an actual attempt. Public rehearsal also risks revealing security gaps and recruiting accomplices.

3) Evidence I can point to: Lucianus’s own messages to me proposing the poisoning-episode and describing the three-stage staging and the deliberate pause; his claim that the idea and funding are his private initiative (which still requires verification); the specificity of his instructions about pause and audience reaction.

4) Immediate risks: a real assault disguised as rehearsal; covert observation of the court’s behavior; escalation of factional tensions if the scene is performed as if targeting the royal family.

5) Concrete recommendations to mitigate risk:
  a) Require the on-stage victim to be entirely fictional and anonymous—do not reference the king’s nephew or any real person.
  b) Forbid any real or convincingly simulated poison. Replace it with unmistakably harmless, symbolic devices (ribbon, colored cloth, mime, sound cue) so no plausible real poisoning can occur.
  c) Remove any staged pause intended to observe reactions; eliminate cues that invite probing the audience or crown.
  d) Prohibit public rehearsals of the scene until safety and intent are certified; confine any necessary rehearsals to a secure, supervised chamber with palace officers present.
  e) Require Lucianus to disclose immediately any sponsors, financiers, or collaborators who backed the scene; verify his claim of sole private funding.
  f) If Lucianus declines disclosure or if evidence points to outside sponsorship or hostile intent, treat the matter as a security issue for the crown and investigate accordingly.
  g) If Your Majesty wishes to preserve the piece as art, authorize a vetted, symbolic rewrite under palace supervision (I can assist drafting safe text and stage directions).

6) Offer of service: I have recorded Lucianus’s messages and refuse to participate in any staging that risks real harm. If Your Majesty approves, I will (i) personally supervise safety and compliance for a harmless version, and/or (ii) conduct discreet inquiries into Lucianus’s backers and intent and report findings to the crown.

I stand ready for Your Majesty’s command.

Horatio: you are appointed stage safety and compliance supervisor; you will oversee one rehearsal and verify the safety measures. I order a single supervised rehearsal now; Horatio shall then state his concerns and the safety protocols briefly to the court before any performance. Lucianus, do not proceed beyond that rehearsal without explicit leave from the Crown. If either of you fails to comply, the scene is forbidden and silence will be enforced to preserve the realm. Keep all remarks measured and avoid naming or accusing ministers in public.

2) Remove any staged pause or cue intended to observe or probe the Crown; eliminate directions that invite audience-testing of reactions.
3) Confine this rehearsal to a secure, supervised chamber with palace officers present; no public rehearsal or unmonitored run-throughs.
4) Require Lucianus to produce in writing any sponsors, financiers, or collaborators and to disclose who will play each role and what props they will use; materials and participants must be vetted before the rehearsal proceeds.
5) Verify identities and readiness of all performers and suspend anyone who refuses compliance.

I will conduct the inspection now, supervise the rehearsal, and then report briefly to the court on the safety protocols and whether further measures or an investigation are necessary. Lucianus: present your written disclosure, your proposed harmless staging, and the actual props now, or the scene remains forbidden. I am ready to begin at the Crown’s command.

The rugged Pyrrhus, he whose sable arms
Black as his purpose, did the night resemble
When he lay couched in the ominous horse,
Hath now this dread and black complexion smear'd
With heraldry more dismal. Head to foot
Now is he total gules; horridly trick'd
With blood of fathers, mothers, daughters, sons,
Bak'd and impasted with the parching streets,
That lend a tyrannous and damned light
To their lord's murder.

But who, O who, had seen the mobled queen,—
Run barefoot up and down, threat'ning the flames
With blinding tears,—and cried out 'O where is he?'
Anon he finds him, striking too short at Greeks;
His antique sword, rebellious to his arm,
Lies where it falls; unequal match'd, Pyrrhus at Priam drives,
In rage strikes wide.

The rugged Pyrrhus, he whose sable arms
Black as his purpose, did the night resemble
When he lay couched in the ominous horse,
Hath now this dread and black complexion smear'd
With heraldry more dismal. Head to foot
Now is he total gules; horridly trick'd
With blood of fathers, mothers, daughters, sons,
Bak'd and impasted with the parching streets,
That lend a tyrannous and damned light
To their lord's murder.

Anon he finds him, striking too short at Greeks;
